1. Where did the man leave his camera?

  • Man: Oh no! I haven’t got my camera!
  • Woman: But you used it just now to take a photograph of the fountain.
  • Man: Oh, I remember, I put it down on the steps while I put my coat on.
  • Woman: Well, let’s drive back quickly – it might still be there.

2. What is the woman’s first memory?

  • Woman: The first thing I remember is when I was about five my father took me to the seaside. My brother stayed at home with my mother because he was too young. We couldn’t go in the sea because it was too rough, but we spent hours playing on the sand.

3. Which train will the woman catch?

  • Woman: What time’s the next train to Manchester please?
  • Man: You’ve just missed the 8.15. The next one’s not until 10.15. There isn’t one at 9.15.
  • Woman: But that’s a two hour wait! and I’ll be late for my appointment at 10.30. But I suppose I haven’t any choice – I’ll go for a coffee while I’m waiting.

4. What should the students take with them tomorrow?

  • Teacher: Now, about the school picnic – it’ll be hot so leave your sweaters behind but make sure you’ve got something to keep the sun off your head, and a drink in case you get thirsty … oh, and something to write on – that’s for a game we’re going to play. And don’t be late!

5. What will they do at the weekend?

  • Woman: What shall we do at the weekend, Tony? The Browns are coming up with their children. I was wondering about a visit to the zoo, or a river trip … or just going down to the sea again …
  • Man: Let’s do something different. The weather should be good, so we could take a picnic to the castle instead. The children will enjoy it and it’ll be a nice change from the beach.
  • Woman: Right then, we’ll do that.

6. What does the woman need to buy?

  • Woman: Let me see, eggs – I’ve got lots of those; butter – I don’t need that. I’ll get some milk, bread, and I’ve nearly finished the toothpaste … oh, there’s a new one in the cupboard. But I do need some apples. Now, where’s my purse?

7. How will the boy get to school?

  • Woman: Get up, Martin. It’s snowed during the night. The school bus won’t be able to go, so you’ll have to walk.
  • Boy: Oh, I’ll go by bike.
  • Woman: Don’t be silly. The snow’s far too deep for that.
  • Boy: Then I’ll ski. That’ll be quicker than walking and I can save the bus fare! But I’ll have some breakfast first.

8. What is the job of Tanya’s boyfriend now?

  • Woman 1: Look – this is the band on the television now, Tanya’s boyfriend is the singer.
  • Woman 2: She told me he played the guitar.
  • Woman 1: He does sometimes, but not tonight, and you know he used to be the keyboard player in that other band. He’s so brilliant. Don’t you think she’s lucky?
  • Woman 2: Oh, I don’t know. I think I prefer the drummer myself, actually.

Conversation 1

  • Interviewer: Simon, tell us about yourself.
  • Simon: Well, like lots of other kids my age, I’ve grown up taking my boat onto the rivers in this area. One of my favourite rivers is (1) the River Stanton, which is fast with excellent white water – so things can get pretty dangerous but it’s exciting and I’m experienced.
  • Interviewer: Now, it was while you were on the River Stanton that you noticed something was wrong.
  • Simon: Yeah, (2) I always wondered why the water made my eyes burn if it got on my face...and why it was a strange, orange colour, especially when the water was running low.
  • Interviewer: So you decided to find out more.
  • Simon: Yeah, I asked other people using the river and (3) I visited a few websites and found out that the river was orange because of pollution from the old mines in the area. There was a lot of mining for coal done in this part of the country. I knew that from my history class at school, but what I didn’t know was that pollution was coming from those old mine works and escaping into the rivers.
  • Interviewer: then you did a qualification, didn’t you?
  • Simon: Yes, I found out about an organization called: “The Friends of the River Stanton”. They told me they did a special course where I could learn how to test the river water to see if it was healthy or not. So that’s what I did and I got really interested in the subject.
  • Interviewer: In fact, you got so interested that you actually started to look for an answer to the pollution problem!
  • Simon: I learned as much as I could about the chemistry behind the pollution. I can’t really explain all the detail, but basically (4) if you add something called limestone to the river, it can improve the chemistry. That means that the plants and fish which had died because of all the mining companies that used to be in the area…could live in the river again. So that made me really happy.

  • Interviewer: Sophie, you’re a native English speaker and you’re been working as a translator for some time now.

  • Sophie: Actually, I don’t have much trouble with those. What’s still quite tricky, though, is when someone mentions a person or an event, perhaps in their country’s history (10).
  • Interviewer: So, do you normally deal with big private firms or with state institutions like local government?
  • Sophie: Well, I was once contacted by an insurance company and I did a job for them, but nearly always it’s a case of an agency asking if I’d be willing to do a particular text (11).
  • Interviewer: That mush speed things up a lot.
  • Sophie: Yes, but it can still be a very long working day. I don’t mind which part of the day I’m working though – that’s one of the advantages of working from home.
  • Interviewer: How do you see the long – term future of translating? Will it continue to be a good area to work in?
  • Sophie: Oh, I think so. Professional standards are higher than they’ve ever been, and the increasingly wide range of languages used internationally means that the demand for high-quality translation will keep growing for many years to come (12).

tasks.tapescript:
Talk 1

I wanna talk about learning languages. I’ve lived in many different countries, both in Western Europe, Middle East, and now here in Hong Kong. And during all of that time, I’ve learned five or six different languages, to one degree or another. I love learning languages, not only are they important when you move to a country, I just find them fascinating.

Before I came to Hong Kong, I lived in Barcelona Spain for ten years. And when I first arrived, the most important thing was being able to communicate with people locally. I don’t attend classes. I don’t think I’m particularly good in classes. I prefer to learn by just talking to people, finding out what I need to say by looking at dictionaries and listening carefully.

Other things that helped me when I first moved to Spain, were watching the typical kinds of programs we see everyday on channels around the world. For example the weather. This is great, because they always say the same things. So you can really quickly hear the same words repeated again and again. And the pictures helped of course.

Other types of program that helped me learn Spanish quickly were things like game shows, where the same thing happens. They have a catchphrase or a slogan that they repeat endlessly when contestants win or when they are called to compete.

As well as that, I used to pick up the Spanish newspapers. First of all, I just accepted that there was no way I was going to understand anything but one or two words. But gradually, I found that I learned lots of new things about this. I was interested because I wanted to know what was happening in the country I lived in. But, I also knew that I could learn a lot of language this way.

So I’d take a dictionary with me sometimes, or I’d notice a word and I’d ask other people what it meant. Anyway, by far the best practice I ever had was just talking to people in the street, or in shops where I’d rehearse in my head what I wanted to say beforehand, before I went in. Usually, I’d make a right mess of it first of all, but, after you get over the embarrassment, it’s quite funny really. And people are very sympathetic and supporting in most cases.

It took me a long time to develop a good level of Spanish. I lived there for ten years, and I think I’m very fluent now. But I think for the first two years I was there, it was quite a struggle to hold a decent conversation. There were always lots of words or expressions that I didn’t pick up. In particular with the colloquial expressions, idioms, that kind of thing, that people use in everyday talk, but you don’t necessarily see written down. I didn’t find those very easy to learn at all. But it was a lot of fun. And people as I said are really supporting when they know that you are genuinely interested in learning their language.

Talk 2

Hello Ladies and Gentleman. It gives me great pleasure to introduce our keynote speaker for today's plenary address, Dr. Howard Miller. Dr. Miller, Professor of Sociology at Washington University, has written numerous articles and books on the issues facing older Americans in our graying society for the past 15 years. Dr. Miller.

Dr. Miller: Thank you for that introduction. Today, I'd like to preface my remarks from a story from my own life which I feel highlights our common concerns that bring us here together.

Several years ago when my grandparents were well into their eighties, they were faced with the reality of no longer being able to adequately care for themselves. My grandfather spoke of his greatest fear, that of leaving the only home they had known for the past 60 years. Fighting back the tears, he spoke proudly of the fact that he had built their home from the ground up, and that he had pounded every nail and laid every brick in the process. The prospect of having to sell their home and give up their independence, and move into a retirement home was an extremely traumatic experience for them. It was, in my grandfather's own words, like having a limb severed off. He was quite emphatic exclaiming that he felt he wasn't important anymore.

For them and some older Americans, their so-called "golden years" are at times not so pleasant, for this period can mean the decline of not only one's health but the loss of identity and self-worth. In many societies, this self-identity is closely related with our social status, occupation, material possessions, or independence.

Furthermore, we often live in societies that value that which is "new" or in vogue, and our own usage of lexicon in the English language often does not bode well for older Americans. I mean how would your family react if you came home tonight elated exclaiming, "Hey, come to the living room and see the OLD black and white TV I brought!" Unfortunately, the word "old" conjures up images of the need to replace or discard.

Now, many of the lectures given at this conference have focused on the issues of pension reform, medical care, and the development of public facilities for senior citizens. And while these are vital issues that must be addressed, I'd like to focus my comments on an underlying issue that will affect the overall success of the other programs mentioned. This has to do with realigning our perspectives on what it means to be a part of this group, and finding meaningful roles the elderly can play and should play in our societies.

First of all, I'd like to talk about ...

Talk 3

Hello. I’m going to talk about British festivals. I’m sure you’ve heard about the Notting Hill Carnival in London and the Edinburgh Festival, but today we’re going to look at a lot more that you might not know about. Actually, a lot of these are not exactly festivals, but strange races or competitions. Some of them are ancient and some are modern.

So, let’s start in January in the north of Scotland with the Burning of the Clavie. This is a whisky barrel which is set alight then carried through the streets as a bonfire. It’s an ancient tradition which always takes place on 11th of January, the first day of the year, according to an older form of the calendar. The bonfire brings good luck for the coming year and people used to keep bits of burnt wood as protection against evil spirits.

At the end of January, even further north, in the Shetland Islands, there’s another fire festival, the Up Helly Aa. This seems like an ancient festival, but has actually only been going for about 130 years – well, it is fairly old, I suppose. People carry fire-lit torches and a Viking boat through the streets, then set fire to the boat. There’s lots of dancing; it’s good fun.

Now to the north of England. On Shrove Tuesday in February, otherwise known as Pancake Day, a special Pancake Bell is rung in Scarborough. Everyone goes down to the road next to the beach where they skip – yep, they jump over long ropes, up to fifteen people to one rope.

And they have pancake races. This is quite common in the UK – running with a frying pan and tossing a pancake at the same time. Another kind of race takes place in spring – cheese rolling. In Gloucestershire, in the south-west of England, round cheeses in round boxes are sent rolling down a hill and people run after them and try and catch them. The hill is very steep, so people often fall over – if you take part in this you need to be very fit and wear your oldest jeans. Nowadays this strange custom attracts visitors from all over the world, but the people from the local village are usually the ones who catch the cheese.

From people-racing, to animals, very tiny animals. World Championship Snail Racing takes place in a village in Norfolk. The snails have to race from an inner circle to an outer circle and the winner gets a lot of lettuce. There’s a party and barbecue for the snail owners and observers. This custom began in the 1960s after a local man saw something similar in France. In the UK we don’t eat snails, by the way.

passage.title: Obesity and the Body Mass Index
passage.text:
Obesity has become one of the most widely discussed public health issues of the past few decades, affecting people in wealthy and developing countries alike. Doctors and researchers needed a simple way to estimate whether a person's weight might pose a risk to their health, and this need led to the widespread adoption of the Body Mass Index, commonly known as BMI. Although the tool was originally developed nearly two hundred years ago by a Belgian mathematician, it did not become a standard part of medical checkups until the twentieth century, when public health officials began searching for numbers that could be compared easily across large populations.

Calculating BMI is fairly simple: a person's weight in kilograms is divided by the square of their height in meters, producing a single number that doctors then place into one of several categories. A result under 18.5 is generally classified as underweight, while a number between 18.5 and 24.9 is considered a healthy range for most adults. Scores from 25 to 29.9 fall into the overweight category, and anything above 30 is classified as obese. Because the calculation requires only two easily measured values, clinics around the world can apply it quickly, without needing expensive equipment or specialized training.

Despite its convenience, BMI has clear limitations that doctors are usually careful to explain to patients. The formula cannot distinguish between muscle and fat, so a highly muscular athlete may receive a BMI score suggesting obesity even though their body fat percentage is quite low. Age, sex, and even ethnicity can also affect how accurately the number reflects true health risk, since fat tends to be distributed differently depending on these factors. For this reason, many doctors now treat BMI as a useful starting point for a conversation rather than a final diagnosis on its own.

The causes of obesity are rarely simple, and researchers generally agree that no single factor explains why rates have risen so sharply in recent decades. Diets higher in processed food and sugar, combined with jobs and daily routines that involve far less physical movement than in previous generations, play an important role. Genetics also matters; some people are more likely than others to gain weight even when eating similar amounts of food. Sleep patterns, stress levels, and even certain medications have additionally been linked to weight gain, making obesity a condition shaped by many overlapping influences rather than a simple failure of willpower.

Carrying excess weight over a long period is associated with a higher risk of several serious conditions, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain types of cancer. Public health campaigns therefore encourage regular exercise, balanced meals, and adequate sleep, though doctors are increasingly careful to frame these recommendations without blaming individuals for a condition shaped by so many outside factors. Some clinics now combine BMI with other simple measurements, such as waist circumference, to build a more complete picture of a patient's health before recommending any changes.

passage.title: Figure Skating: Between Sport and Art
passage.text:
Few Olympic disciplines provoke as much debate over classification as figure skating, an activity that sits, somewhat uneasily, at the intersection of competitive sport and performing art. Skaters must execute jumps, spins, and footwork sequences that demand years of highly technical training, yet they are simultaneously expected to convey musicality, emotion, and narrative in a way that few other Olympic events require. Whether this duality strengthens figure skating's appeal or simply complicates how audiences and judges alike are supposed to evaluate it remains, even among longtime fans, an unresolved question.

The physical toll of elite figure skating is often underestimated by casual viewers who see only the finished performance rather than the years of preparation behind it. A single quadruple jump, now common among top competitors, generates forces on landing that can exceed several times the skater's body weight, and repeated exposure to such impact has been linked to stress fractures and chronic joint problems that sometimes end careers well before an athlete reaches their physical prime. Coaches increasingly balance ambitious technical content against injury risk, a calculation that has become considerably more difficult as competitors push jump difficulty ever higher in pursuit of higher scores.

Scoring in figure skating combines a technical score, based on the difficulty and execution of specific elements, with a component score meant to capture artistry, interpretation, and overall presentation, and it is this second component that has generated the most persistent controversy. Critics argue that artistic scoring, however carefully judges are trained, inevitably introduces a degree of subjectivity that pure timing or distance-based sports largely avoid, opening the door to accusations of national bias or inconsistent standards between competitions. Federation officials have tried to address such accusations by rotating judging panels between events, though skaters say they remain skeptical that the change has meaningfully reduced bias. Defenders of the current system counter that some subjectivity is unavoidable, and arguably even desirable, in any discipline that claims to reward artistic merit rather than technical execution alone.

Television audiences for major figure skating events, particularly at the Winter Olympics, have historically outpaced those for several other winter sports combined, and this popularity has shaped the sport's development in ways that extend well beyond the rink itself. Broadcasters favor programming that generates strong emotional narratives, and skaters who successfully cultivate a compelling public persona often attract sponsorship deals considerably larger than their competitive rankings alone would predict. Some sport administrators worry that this dynamic quietly rewards charisma and marketability over pure technical achievement, subtly shifting incentives in a sport already criticized for the ambiguity of its scoring.

Mental health concerns among competitive skaters, while not unique to the sport, appear to be intensified by factors that are somewhat distinctive to figure skating's particular structure. The subjective nature of artistic scoring may leave athletes feeling that their fate rests partly on factors beyond their direct control, a sense of powerlessness that sports psychologists suggest can heighten anxiety more than sports where performance is measured by an objective clock or scoreboard. Extremely young competitive ages in some disciplines, though gradually being addressed through revised eligibility rules, have additionally drawn concern from researchers who study the long-term effects of intense early specialization on adolescent athletes.

Looking forward, several skating federations have begun experimenting with technology intended to reduce, though probably never fully eliminate, the subjectivity embedded in artistic scoring. Motion-tracking systems capable of measuring rotation speed, jump height, and landing quality with far greater precision than a human eye could offer one avenue for standardizing technical evaluation, even as most officials acknowledge that no algorithm currently exists that can meaningfully assess artistry or emotional expression. Whether such tools ultimately narrow the gap between figure skating's athletic and artistic identities, or merely relocate the debate to a new technical frontier, remains very much an open question within the sport.

passage.title: The Elusive Causes of Crime
passage.text:
Crime has occupied criminologists, economists, and policymakers for well over a century, yet consensus on its fundamental causes remains elusive despite an extraordinary volume of accumulated research. Part of the difficulty lies in the sheer diversity of behaviors the term encompasses, ranging from impulsive acts of violence to meticulously planned financial fraud, each of which may respond to entirely different explanatory frameworks and, by extension, different policy interventions. Any attempt to reduce crime to a single cause, however intuitively appealing, tends to collapse once tested against the messy variability of actual criminal behavior across different societies and historical periods.

Two broad theoretical traditions have long dominated the field, though neither has fully displaced the other. Classical criminology, rooted in eighteenth-century philosophy, treats offenders as rational actors who weigh potential gains against the likelihood and severity of punishment, a framework that continues to underpin much contemporary sentencing policy. Positivist criminology, by contrast, locates the roots of criminal behavior in factors substantially outside an individual's immediate control — psychological disposition, social environment, or even, according to some contested strands of research, biological predisposition — implying that punishment alone addresses only the symptom rather than the underlying cause.

Empirical support for purely economic explanations of crime is considerably more mixed than early theorists assumed it would be. While concentrated poverty and stark income inequality correlate with elevated crime rates across numerous studies, the relationship is neither uniform nor straightforwardly causal; some economically disadvantaged communities exhibit remarkably low crime rates, a pattern researchers increasingly attribute to the strength of local social networks and informal community oversight rather than to income levels themselves. This suggests that economic deprivation may function less as a direct trigger and more as one condition among several that, in combination, raise the probability of criminal behavior.

Predictive policing tools, which use historical crime data to forecast where future offenses are statistically likely to occur, have been adopted by numerous police departments on the promise of allocating scarce resources more efficiently — and the underlying premise, however contested its execution has proven, is not without a degree of empirical justification. Departments using such systems in several pilot programs reported modest reductions in certain property-crime categories within targeted zones, though whether these gains reflect genuine crime prevention or merely displacement of criminal activity into neighboring, unmonitored areas remains a question the existing data cannot fully resolve.

Critics of predictive policing raise a concern that goes well beyond simple accuracy: because the algorithms are trained on historical arrest data, and because policing has historically been concentrated more heavily in certain neighborhoods regardless of actual underlying crime rates, the resulting predictions risk reproducing and even amplifying prior patterns of disproportionate enforcement rather than correcting for them. Such a feedback loop, once established, may prove difficult to detect from within the system itself, since each cycle of concentrated policing generates precisely the kind of arrest data that appears, superficially, to validate the original prediction.

Whether punitive deterrence or rehabilitative intervention more effectively reduces reoffending remains a genuinely contested empirical question rather than a settled matter of ideology, and the picture that recidivism research paints resists simple summary. Programs emphasizing education, vocational training, and mental health treatment during incarceration have, in several long-term studies, been associated with meaningfully lower reoffending rates than sentencing length alone would predict, yet the same body of research cautions that these effects vary considerably depending on program quality, participant selection, and the availability of post-release support — variables that are frequently under-reported in studies claiming broad success.

Taken together, the accumulated evidence resists any tidy narrative in which a single cause, or a single remedy, adequately explains criminal behavior or its prevention. Crime appears instead as an outcome shaped by the interaction of individual circumstance, community structure, and institutional response, an interaction complex enough that even well-designed interventions produce effects that vary substantially depending on context. Policymakers who treat any single theory as sufficient, whether classical, positivist, or purely technological, do so, the evidence suggests, at the cost of overlooking precisely the complexity that decades of criminological research have worked to establish.

passage.title: Solar Power's Uncertain Trajectory
passage.text:
Solar photovoltaic technology has moved, within roughly two decades, from a niche and heavily subsidized energy source to one of the cheapest forms of new electricity generation in much of the world, a trajectory that few energy analysts anticipated with any confidence as recently as the early 2000s. Not only has the cost of manufacturing solar panels fallen dramatically, but the pace of that decline has itself accelerated in ways that continue to outstrip even relatively optimistic industry forecasts, complicating any attempt to project the technology's trajectory more than a few years into the future with real precision.

The physical efficiency of converting sunlight into electricity remains bound by thermodynamic limits that no amount of engineering can fully overcome, though commercially available panels still operate well below even these theoretical ceilings, leaving meaningful room for incremental improvement. Laboratory prototypes using multi-junction cell designs have achieved efficiencies exceeding forty percent under concentrated light, a figure that may eventually filter down into mass-market products, though the manufacturing costs associated with such designs currently make widespread commercial deployment appear, at best, a distant and uncertain prospect rather than an imminent one.

Manufacturing a solar panel is not, in itself, an environmentally costless process, and critics of overly enthusiastic solar advocacy are right to note that producing silicon wafers, purifying raw materials, and assembling finished panels all consume considerable energy, some of it still drawn from fossil-fuel sources depending on where manufacturing occurs. Most life-cycle analyses conclude that a typical panel generates enough clean electricity within one to four years to offset the energy invested in producing it, after which the remaining twenty-plus years of its operational life represent a genuine net energy gain — though this payback estimate, researchers caution, varies considerably depending on the panel's manufacturing location and the carbon intensity of that region's electrical grid.

Grid operators increasingly regard the intermittent nature of solar generation as the technology's most consequential limitation, and this concern is not merely theoretical: several regions with high solar penetration have already documented significant operational strain during the transition hours around sunset, when solar output drops sharply just as residential electricity demand typically rises. Battery storage technology, while advancing rapidly, has not yet reached a cost point at which utility-scale deployment can fully resolve this mismatch everywhere, leaving many grid operators to rely on a patchwork of natural-gas peaker plants, demand-response programs, and imported power to smooth over the gap, at least for the foreseeable near term.

Whether solar energy's continued cost decline can be attributed primarily to manufacturing scale, to genuine technological innovation, or to sustained government subsidies remains a matter that economists studying the industry have not fully settled, and the honest answer likely involves some combination of all three operating simultaneously rather than any single dominant factor. Removing subsidies abruptly in markets where they remain substantial could, some analysts argue, slow adoption meaningfully in the short term, even if underlying manufacturing costs continue to fall regardless of policy support, a distinction that matters considerably for how policymakers ought to plan any eventual subsidy phase-out.

Large-scale solar installations inevitably compete with agriculture, wildlife habitat, and other forms of land use, a tension that has grown more visible as utility-scale solar farms have expanded into rural areas previously used for farming or left as open space. Some research suggests that carefully designed 'agrivoltaic' systems, which combine solar panels with compatible crops or grazing livestock on the same land, may substantially reduce this competition, though such dual-use approaches remain far less common than conventional single-use solar farms and their economic viability across diverse crop types has not been thoroughly established.

Taken as a whole, solar energy's future contribution to global electricity generation appears to hinge less on any single technological breakthrough than on the simultaneous resolution of several distinct challenges — storage economics, manufacturing decarbonization, land-use tension, and policy design — none of which can be fully addressed in isolation from the others. Analysts who forecast solar's near-total dominance of future electricity markets, and those who dismiss it as fundamentally limited by intermittency, arguably both overstate the degree of certainty that current evidence actually supports.

tasks.suggestion:
Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

  • Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q4, R4Q8): Sử dụng kỹ năng Scanning (Đọc quét từ khóa) để tìm kiếm chính xác vị trí dữ kiện trong bài đọc:
    • Với R4Q2, quét từ khóa "thermodynamic limits" hoặc "commercially available" ở đoạn 2 để tìm khẳng định đúng về tiềm năng cải thiện hiệu suất của pin mặt trời thương mại.
    • Với R4Q4, quét cụm từ "payback estimate" hoặc "varies" ở đoạn 3 để xác định hai yếu tố ảnh hưởng trực tiếp đến thời gian hoàn vốn năng lượng (vị trí sản xuất và cường độ phát thải carbon của lưới điện).
    • Với R4Q8, quét từ khóa "agrivoltaic" ở đoạn 6 để tìm thực trạng triển khai hệ thống kết hợp nông nghiệp và điện mặt trời (giúp giảm xung đột đất đai nhưng vẫn ít phổ biến).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R4Q3, R4Q9): Áp dụng kỹ thuật Context Clues (Manh mối ngữ cảnh):
    • Với R4Q3, xét ngữ cảnh đoạn 1 mô tả tốc độ giảm chi phí diễn ra nhanh vượt xa cả những dự báo lạc quan nhất để chọn từ đồng nghĩa cho "outstrip".
    • Với R4Q9, xét ngữ cảnh đoạn 4 nhấn mạnh tính chập chờn của điện mặt trời là hạn chế lớn nhất/quan trọng nhất mà các đơn vị vận hành lưới điện phải đối mặt để tìm từ đồng nghĩa cho "consequential".
  • Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R4Q5): Đọc câu trước câu chứa cụm "this mismatch" ở đoạn 4 để xác định sự chênh lệch/mất cân đối giữa sản lượng điện mặt trời sụt giảm vào lúc hoàng hôn và nhu cầu tiêu thụ điện tăng cao của người dân.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R4Q6): Đối soát các giải pháp ứng phó được đề cập ở đoạn 4 (nhà máy điện khí tự nhiên, chương trình điều chỉnh phụ tải, điện nhập khẩu) để chỉ ra giải pháp không hề được nhắc đến.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R4Q7): Kết hợp phân tích ở đoạn 5 về việc các nhà kinh tế học chưa thống nhất nguyên nhân chính (quy mô sản xuất, đổi mới công nghệ hay trợ cấp) để chọn đáp án phản ánh sự kết hợp đồng thời của nhiều yếu tố.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính & Thái độ tác giả (R4Q1, R4Q10): Phân tích bức tranh tổng thể của văn bản:
    • Với R4Q1, tổng hợp ý tưởng chính ở đoạn cuối khẳng định tương lai của năng lượng mặt trời phụ thuộc vào việc giải quyết đồng thời nhiều thách thức liên quan.
    • Với R4Q10, nhận diện quan điểm của tác giả khi chỉ ra cả dự báo quá lạc quan lẫn quá bi quan đều thổi phồng mức độ chắc chắn để chọn đánh giá thái độ hoài nghi mang tính cân bằng (Skeptical of both).

Lời khuyên: Hãy bắt đầu bằng việc xử lý nhanh các câu hỏi định vị rõ ràng như Quy chiếu (R4Q5) và Từ vựng (R4Q3, R4Q9). Tiếp đó, sử dụng kỹ năng đọc quét dữ kiện cho các câu Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q4, R4Q8) và câu Loại trừ (R4Q6). Sau cùng, dựa trên bức tranh thông tin toàn cảnh đã ráp nối, bạn sẽ dễ dàng lựa chọn phương án chính xác cho các câu đòi hỏi tư duy tổng hợp gồm Suy luận (R4Q7), Thái độ tác giả (R4Q10) và Ý chính toàn bài (R4Q1).

tasks.title:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. You recently received an email from your friend, Jimmy, who is thinking about taking a Chinese course.

He asked you about the Chinese class you are attending. Read part of his email below.
tasks.content:
I heard you've been taking a Chinese class recently, and I'm thinking of signing up too. Could you tell me more about it?

  • What is the class like?
  • How much is the tuition fee?
  • What do you think of the teacher?
tasks.description: Respond to Jimmy's email and answer all of his questions. You should write at least 120 words. You don't need to include your name or addresses. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfillment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng đề:

Đây là dạng Informal Email gửi cho bạn bè, chia sẻ trải nghiệm cá nhân về một lớp học. Bạn cần trả lời đầy đủ 3 câu hỏi chính của Jimmy: lớp học như thế nào, học phí bao nhiêu, và cảm nghĩ về giáo viên. Yêu cầu tối thiểu 120 từ, giọng văn thân mật, tự nhiên như đang chia sẻ trải nghiệm thật với bạn bè.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục logic (Organization):

  • Greeting: Chào hỏi thân mật. Ví dụ: Dear Jimmy,
  • Opening: Bày tỏ sự vui mừng khi nhận được thư. Ví dụ: I was so happy to hear that you're considering taking a Chinese class too!
  • Body 1 (Class): Mô tả lớp học. Ví dụ: The class is quite small, with about ten students, so we get plenty of chances to practice speaking.
  • Body 2 (Fee): Nêu học phí cụ thể. Ví dụ: The tuition fee is around 2 million VND for a three-month course.
  • Body 3 (Teacher): Chia sẻ cảm nghĩ về giáo viên. Ví dụ: As for the teacher, she's really patient and explains grammar points very clearly.
  • Closing: Khuyến khích bạn tham gia. Ví dụ: I really think you'd enjoy it, so let me know if you decide to join!
  • Sign-off: Best wishes, [Your Name].

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

Sử dụng thì Hiện tại đơn để mô tả thói quen, đặc điểm lớp học và giáo viên. Kết hợp tính từ miêu tả cảm xúc, tính cách để bài viết sinh động, chân thực hơn.

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • Tuition fee: Học phí
  • Native speaker: Người bản xứ
  • Patient teacher: Giáo viên kiên nhẫn
  • Small class size: Lớp học sĩ số nhỏ
  • Interactive lesson: Bài học tương tác
  • Fluent in Chinese: Thành thạo tiếng Trung
  • Enrol in a course: Đăng ký khóa học

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • First of all: Trước hết
  • As for: Còn về
  • Besides: Bên cạnh đó
  • Overall: Nhìn chung
  • By the way: Nhân tiện

Cách diễn đạt cảm xúc (Expressing feelings):

  • I was so happy to hear...: Tôi rất vui khi nghe...
  • I really enjoy...: Tôi thực sự thích...
  • I think you'd love it!: Tôi nghĩ bạn sẽ thích nó!

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ trả lời 1-2 trong số 3 câu hỏi mà đề bài yêu cầu.
  • Mô tả quá chung chung, không có chi tiết cụ thể về lớp học, học phí, giáo viên.
  • Quên phần chào hỏi hoặc kết thư.

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 2 phút cuối:

  • Đếm lại số từ, đảm bảo đạt tối thiểu 120 từ.
  • Kiểm tra đã trả lời đủ cả 3 câu hỏi của Jimmy chưa.
  • Rà soát lỗi chính tả và cách dùng thì.

6. Tư duy làm bài:

Hãy viết như thể bạn đang thật sự kể cho một người bạn nghe về lớp học của mình. Sự chân thực, cụ thể trong ví dụ sẽ giúp bài viết tự nhiên và thuyết phục hơn.

tasks.title: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
tasks.content:
Advertising has become an inseparable part of modern life, appearing on television, social media, billboards, and almost every website people visit.

While advertising helps businesses promote their products and informs consumers about new options, some people believe it also has several negative effects on society and individuals.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of advertising.
tasks.description: Write an essay to an educated reader to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of advertising. Include reasons and any relevant examples to support your answer. You should write at least 250 words. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfilment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng bài:

Đây là dạng bài Advantages and Disadvantages Essay, yêu cầu bạn phân tích cả mặt lợi và mặt hại của quảng cáo trong đời sống hiện đại. Bạn cần trình bày cân bằng cả hai khía cạnh, có thể nêu quan điểm cá nhân ở phần kết luận. Yêu cầu tối thiểu 250 từ, tránh chỉ tập trung vào một phía.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục (Organization):

  • Introduction: Giới thiệu vai trò của quảng cáo trong đời sống hiện đại. Ví dụ: Advertising has become an integral part of everyday life, influencing how people shop and make decisions.
  • Body 1 (Advantages): Topic sentence → Explanation → Example. Ví dụ: One major advantage of advertising is that it provides consumers with useful information about new products and services.
  • Body 2 (Disadvantages): Ví dụ: However, advertising also has notable drawbacks, such as encouraging unnecessary spending and sometimes conveying misleading information.
  • Body 3 (Ý kiến cá nhân, nếu có): Ví dụ: In my opinion, while advertising offers real benefits, stricter regulations are needed to prevent misleading claims.
  • Conclusion: Tóm lại cả hai mặt. Ví dụ: In conclusion, although advertising brings certain benefits to both businesses and consumers, its potential drawbacks should not be overlooked.

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

Sử dụng thì Hiện tại đơn để nêu sự thật chung, kết hợp cấu trúc so sánh và nhượng bộ (although, despite) để liên kết hai mặt lợi - hại một cách mạch lạc. Có câu Thesis Statement rõ ràng ở phần mở bài.

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • Consumer awareness: Nhận thức của người tiêu dùng
  • Brand recognition: Nhận diện thương hiệu
  • Misleading information: Thông tin sai lệch
  • Impulse buying: Mua sắm bốc đồng
  • Market competition: Cạnh tranh thị trường
  • Targeted advertising: Quảng cáo nhắm mục tiêu
  • Consumerism: Chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • On the positive side / On the other hand: Về mặt tích cực / Mặt khác (Thêm ý)
  • However / Nevertheless: Tuy nhiên (Đối lập)
  • As a result / Consequently: Do đó (Nguyên nhân - kết quả)
  • For example / For instance: Ví dụ như (Minh họa)
  • Despite this: Mặc dù vậy (Nhượng bộ)
  • In conclusion / Overall: Nhìn chung (Kết luận)

Diễn đạt lại ý (Paraphrasing):

  • Promotional content: Thay cho "advertising".
  • Excessive spending habits: Thay cho "unnecessary spending".
  • The general public: Thay cho "consumers".

Cách diễn đạt ý kiến / so sánh:

  • One clear benefit is...: Một lợi ích rõ ràng là...
  • Compared to its drawbacks...: So với những hạn chế của nó...
  • From my point of view...: Theo quan điểm của tôi...

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ tập trung liệt kê lợi ích hoặc chỉ hạn chế, thiếu cân bằng cả hai mặt.
  • Không có ví dụ cụ thể minh họa cho từng luận điểm.
  • Kết luận lặp lại y nguyên câu mở bài mà không tổng hợp lại ý.

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 3–5 phút cuối:

  • Kiểm tra xem cả lợi ích và hạn chế đều được trình bày cân đối.
  • Đảm bảo bài viết đạt tối thiểu 250 từ.
  • Rà soát lỗi ngữ pháp và tính liên kết giữa các đoạn văn.

6. Tư duy làm bài:

Hãy giữ thái độ khách quan khi phân tích, tránh thiên vị quá mức về một phía. Mỗi luận điểm nên đi kèm ví dụ thực tế để bài viết có sức thuyết phục cao hơn.

questions: Do you often take breaks during work or study?
What do you usually do during your breaks?
How important do you think breaks are for productivity?
Do you prefer indoor or outdoor activities?
What do you usually do in your office during your free time?
Do you think a comfortable workplace affects how well you perform?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Phần thi này kéo dài 3 phút với 6 câu hỏi, được giám khảo hỏi trực tiếp theo hình thức hội thoại tự nhiên.
  • Chủ đề A (Giờ nghỉ giải lao): Ba câu hỏi đầu xoay quanh thói quen nghỉ giải lao, hoạt động trong giờ nghỉ và tầm quan trọng của việc nghỉ ngơi với hiệu suất làm việc.
  • Chủ đề B (Hoạt động trong/ngoài trời và nơi làm việc): Ba câu hỏi sau khai thác sở thích hoạt động trong nhà hay ngoài trời, thói quen trong văn phòng và ảnh hưởng của môi trường làm việc.
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm gồm: Độ trôi chảy (Fluency), Từ vựng (Vocabulary), Ngữ pháp (Grammar) và Phát âm (Pronunciation).
  • Nên phân bổ khoảng 25–30 giây cho mỗi câu hỏi, tránh dồn quá nhiều thời gian cho một chủ đề.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Áp dụng cấu trúc Answer – Reason – Example (ARE): trả lời trực tiếp, đưa lý do, sau đó minh họa bằng ví dụ cụ thể.
  • Ví dụ Chủ đề A: "Yes, I usually take a short break every two hours because it helps me stay focused and avoid mental fatigue."
  • Ví dụ Chủ đề B: "I prefer indoor activities like reading, but I try to spend time outdoors on weekends to get some fresh air."
  • Luôn tự hỏi Why?/How? sau mỗi câu trả lời ngắn để mở rộng ý (bắt buộc).
  • Dùng một câu chuyển ý ngắn gọn khi chuyển từ Chủ đề A sang B, ví dụ: "Now, let's move on to how I spend my time at the workplace..." (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Giữ tốc độ nói đều, sử dụng các từ đệm tự nhiên như "well", "actually" để tránh im lặng kéo dài.
  • Về thì: dùng hiện tại đơn khi nói về thói quen nghỉ ngơi và hoạt động trong/ngoài trời ("I usually...", "I tend to..."), dùng hiện tại hoàn thành nếu nhắc đến trải nghiệm tích lũy ("I have noticed that short breaks improve my focus").
  • Nếu quên từ, hãy diễn giải bằng cách mô tả (paraphrase) thay vì dừng lại.
  • Từ vựng Chủ đề A: take a breather (nghỉ giải lao ngắn), mental fatigue (mệt mỏi tinh thần), boost productivity (tăng năng suất), step away from the desk (rời khỏi bàn làm việc).
  • Từ vựng Chủ đề B: get some fresh air (hít thở không khí trong lành), a cozy workspace (không gian làm việc ấm cúng), stay indoors (ở trong nhà), a comfortable environment (môi trường thoải mái).

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • recharge my energy (nạp lại năng lượng) — Chủ đề A.
  • avoid burnout (tránh kiệt sức) — Chủ đề A.
  • a well-deserved rest (một khoảng nghỉ xứng đáng) — Chủ đề A.
  • a change of scenery (thay đổi không gian) — Chủ đề B.
  • foster creativity (thúc đẩy sự sáng tạo) — Chủ đề B.
  • a well-organized office (văn phòng được sắp xếp gọn gàng) — Chủ đề B.

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • Actually, – mở đầu ý kiến cá nhân tự nhiên (thực ra thì).
  • In terms of... – giới hạn phạm vi câu trả lời (về mặt...).
  • Apart from that, – bổ sung ý (bên cạnh đó).
  • The main reason is that... – nêu lý do chính.
  • Speaking of... – chuyển chủ đề mượt mà (nói đến...).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "Personally, I think regular breaks are essential for maintaining focus throughout the day." (Cá nhân tôi nghĩ...) — Chủ đề A.
  • "From my point of view, short walks during breaks work better than staying on my phone." (Theo quan điểm của tôi...) — Chủ đề A.
  • "As far as I'm concerned, a comfortable workplace has a direct impact on how productive I feel." (Theo tôi thì...) — Chủ đề B.

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Trả lời cụt lủn kiểu "Yes" hoặc "Indoor" mà không giải thích thêm — đây là lỗi nghiêm trọng nhất.
  • Với Chủ đề A: chỉ nói "I take breaks" mà không mô tả cụ thể mình làm gì trong lúc nghỉ.
  • Với Chủ đề B: nhầm lẫn giữa "in the office" và "at the office", hoặc không phân biệt rõ giữa sở thích và thói quen thực tế.
  • Dùng sai thì, ví dụ dùng thì tương lai khi mô tả thói quen hiện tại.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Dùng câu chêm: "That's an interesting question, let me think for a moment" để có thêm thời gian.
  • Nếu quên từ vựng cụ thể, hãy mô tả bằng từ đơn giản hơn, ví dụ thay vì "break room" có thể nói "a place where employees can rest during work".
  • Với Chủ đề A, nếu không nhớ chi tiết, có thể nói chung chung về "a short rest to clear my mind" rồi phát triển thêm.
  • Với Chủ đề B, nếu bí ý tưởng, hãy liên hệ đến cảm giác thoải mái khi làm việc trong một không gian dễ chịu.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Hãy xem đây như một cuộc trò chuyện thân mật, không phải một bài kiểm tra căng thẳng.
  • Khi chuyển từ Chủ đề A sang B, hãy "reset" tâm lý và coi đó là một câu hỏi hoàn toàn mới.
  • Ưu tiên sự tự nhiên và trôi chảy hơn là cố gắng dùng từ vựng học thuật phức tạp.

tasks.situation:
Your family is choosing an elementary school for your younger sister.

You are considering the following options:

  • Option 1: A private school
  • Option 2: An international school
  • Option 3: A public school

Choose the best option and explain your reasons.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Tình huống: gia đình bạn đang chọn trường tiểu học cho em gái.
  • Ba lựa chọn: trường tư thục (private school), trường quốc tế (international school), và trường công lập (public school).
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm: khả năng phân tích, so sánh và đưa ra kết luận thuyết phục, cùng với Fluency, Vocabulary, Grammar và Pronunciation.
  • Thời gian: 4 phút — khoảng 1 phút chuẩn bị và 3 phút trình bày.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc I-C-E (Introduction – Comparison/Body – End): giới thiệu tình huống, phân tích lần lượt ba lựa chọn, sau đó kết luận và đưa ra lý do.
  • Option 1 (trường tư): "A private school usually offers smaller class sizes and more personalized attention, but the tuition fees can be quite high."
  • Option 2 (trường quốc tế): "An international school provides a strong foreign language environment and modern facilities, though it is often the most expensive choice."
  • Option 3 (trường công): "A public school is affordable and close to home, but class sizes tend to be larger, which may reduce individual attention."
  • Mẹo: luôn neo lập luận vào bối cảnh thực tế của một gia đình đang cân nhắc học phí và chất lượng giáo dục (bắt buộc).
  • Mẹo: dùng từ nối tương phản như "however", "on the other hand" để chuyển giữa ưu và nhược điểm (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Liên kết ba lựa chọn với nhau thay vì nói tách biệt, ví dụ: "Compared to Option 3, Option 2 offers a more international learning environment."
  • Về thì: dùng câu điều kiện loại 1 khi dự đoán hệ quả ("If she attends an international school, she will improve her English quickly") và hiện tại đơn khi mô tả đặc điểm từng loại trường.
  • Paraphrase cụm "choose a school" thành "select an educational institution" hoặc "decide on a school" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • personalized attention (sự quan tâm cá nhân hóa).
  • tuition fees (học phí).
  • a well-rounded education (nền giáo dục toàn diện).
  • modern facilities (cơ sở vật chất hiện đại).
  • class size (sĩ số lớp học).
  • within a reasonable budget (trong ngân sách hợp lý).

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • On the other hand, – nêu quan điểm đối lập (mặt khác).
  • Compared to..., – so sánh giữa các lựa chọn.
  • Taking everything into account, – tổng kết trước khi kết luận (xét tổng thể).
  • Nevertheless, – nhấn mạnh điểm trái ngược (tuy nhiên).
  • As a result, – nêu hệ quả (kết quả là).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "If it were up to me, I would choose the private school because it balances quality and cost reasonably well." (Nếu là tôi...)
  • "I would strongly recommend the international school if the family can afford the tuition." (Tôi sẽ khuyên...)
  • "In my opinion, the public school is a practical choice for families with a limited budget." (Theo ý kiến của tôi...)

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ khen lựa chọn mình chọn mà không chỉ ra nhược điểm của các lựa chọn còn lại.
  • Lặp đi lặp lại từ "good"/"expensive" thay vì dùng tính từ học thuật hơn như "beneficial", "costly".
  • Không đưa ra kết luận rõ ràng ở cuối bài nói.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Nếu quên từ vựng chuyên ngành giáo dục, chuyển hướng sang yếu tố chi phí hoặc khoảng cách để tiếp tục lập luận.
  • Dùng câu chêm: "Let's evaluate this option from a different perspective" để có thêm thời gian suy nghĩ.
  • Nếu bí ý ở một lựa chọn, hãy bình tĩnh chuyển sang phân tích lựa chọn tiếp theo.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Hãy suy nghĩ như một người thân trong gia đình đang thực sự cân nhắc cho việc học của em gái.
  • Đưa ra một vài gợi ý cải thiện ngay cả cho lựa chọn được chọn để thể hiện tư duy phản biện.
  • Sự mạch lạc và logic trong lập luận quan trọng hơn việc dùng từ vựng phức tạp.

tasks.topic: The benefits of investment in the arts

mindmap.title: Benefits of Investment in the Arts
ideas: Contributing to cultural growth and preservation
Boosting economic development through creative industries

followUp: How can governments encourage more investment in the arts?
Do you think art education should be compulsory in schools?
What role do the arts play in shaping a country's international image?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Chủ đề: Lợi ích của việc đầu tư vào nghệ thuật, với 3 nhánh ý chính và 1 nhánh ý cá nhân (gợi ý nhánh thứ 4: nghệ thuật giúp nâng cao đời sống tinh thần của cộng đồng).
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm: khả năng phát triển ý mạch lạc theo sơ đồ tư duy, cùng Fluency, Vocabulary, Grammar và Pronunciation.
  • Thời gian: 5 phút; khoảng 3–3.5 phút cho bài nói chính, phần còn lại dành cho câu hỏi follow-up.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc IDEA (Introduction – Detail – Example – Add/wrap up) vì chủ đề mang tính xã hội và kinh tế, cần cả lý lẽ lẫn ví dụ thực tế.
  • Ví dụ 1 (mở bài): "Investing in the arts brings a wide range of benefits, from personal development to national economic growth."
  • Ví dụ 2 (nhánh cá nhân): "Personally, I believe that the arts also play a role in improving people's mental well-being by providing a creative outlet for self-expression."
  • Mẹo: khi nói về từng nhánh ý, hãy đưa ra một ví dụ cụ thể như một lễ hội nghệ thuật hoặc ngành công nghiệp sáng tạo để minh họa.
  • Mẹo: bám sát sơ đồ tư duy để tránh lan man, không lặp lại ý đã nói (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Dùng cụm từ chuyển tiếp mượt mà giữa các nhánh ý, ví dụ "Another significant benefit is...".
  • Về thì: dùng hiện tại đơn để nêu sự thật/quan điểm chung ("The creative industry contributes significantly to the economy") và hiện tại hoàn thành để nói về trải nghiệm tích lũy ("I have taken part in several art workshops").
  • Paraphrase "investment in the arts" bằng "funding for the arts" hoặc "supporting artistic activities" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • nurture creativity (nuôi dưỡng sự sáng tạo).
  • preserve cultural heritage (bảo tồn di sản văn hóa).
  • the creative industry (ngành công nghiệp sáng tạo).
  • generate revenue (tạo ra doanh thu).
  • a source of national pride (niềm tự hào dân tộc).
  • enhance quality of life (nâng cao chất lượng cuộc sống).

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • To begin with, – mở đầu nhánh ý đầu tiên (trước hết).
  • Moreover, – bổ sung ý (hơn nữa).
  • Another point worth noting is... – chuyển sang nhánh ý mới.
  • In addition to that, – mở rộng ý (thêm vào đó).
  • To sum up, – kết luận (tóm lại).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "I would say that investing in the arts is just as important as investing in science or technology." (Tôi cho rằng...)
  • "From what I've seen, countries with strong art industries often enjoy a more positive international image." (Theo những gì tôi quan sát được...)
  • "It seems to me that supporting local artists helps preserve traditions that might otherwise be lost." (Đối với tôi thì có vẻ như...)

4. Gợi ý trả lời câu hỏi follow-up:

  • "How can governments encourage more investment in the arts?" – By offering grants, tax incentives, and public funding for artists and cultural institutions.
  • "Do you think art education should be compulsory in schools?" – Yes, because it nurtures creativity and helps students develop skills beyond academic subjects.
  • "What role do the arts play in shaping a country's international image?" – The arts showcase a nation's culture and creativity, helping to attract tourism and build cultural diplomacy.

5. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ liệt kê ý mà không giải thích hoặc cho ví dụ cụ thể.
  • Quên nhánh ý cá nhân — nên chuẩn bị trước một quan điểm riêng liên quan đến nghệ thuật.
  • Dành quá nhiều thời gian cho bài nói chính, không còn thời gian trả lời follow-up.

6. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Neo vào một hoạt động nghệ thuật thực tế mà bản thân từng tham gia hoặc chứng kiến khi bí ý.
  • Câu chêm học thuật: "That is a complex issue. If we evaluate it from a societal viewpoint..."
  • Nếu quên từ vựng chuyên ngành, dùng mô tả đơn giản, ví dụ thay vì "patronage" có thể nói "financial support given to artists".

7. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Suy nghĩ từ góc nhìn của cả cá nhân, xã hội và nền kinh tế khi đánh giá lợi ích của nghệ thuật.
  • Sự mạch lạc và logic trong luồng ý là yếu tố then chốt để đạt điểm cao.
  • Đừng cố nhồi nhét từ vựng khó, hãy ưu tiên truyền tải ý tưởng rõ ràng và tự nhiên.
